entries.79a2cb82e06c57ed1ccd0ea9d993b83ba8919c47: <div eID="gen24515" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24516" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24517" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24517" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24516" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24518" type="x-p"/> The king's heart is in the hand of God. We should practice mercy and justice. The lying tongue. The quarrelsome woman. The punishment of the wicked. The uncharitable. The private gift. The happiness of the righteous. The wicked a ransom for the righteous. The treasures of the wise. He who guards his tongue. Desire of the sluggard. The false witness. Salvation is of the Lord. <div eID="gen24518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24519" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24520" type="x-p"/> The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord - The Lord is the only ruler of princes. He alone can govern and direct their counsels. But there is an allusion here to the Eastern method of watering their lands. Several canals are dug from one stream; and by opening a particular sluice, the husbandman can direct a stream to whatever part he please: so the king's heart, wherever it turns; i.e., to whomsoever he is disposed to show favor. As the land is enriched with the streams employed in irrigation; so is the favourite of the king, by the royal bounty: and God can induce the king to give that bounty to whomsoever he will. See Harmer.
entries.d886aafa4ef373d1a2375821f77d2659230bcc99: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24521" type="x-p"/> The Lord pondereth the hearts - Every man feels strongly attached to his own opinions, modes of acting, etc.; and though he will not easily give up any thing to the judgment of a neighbor, whom he will naturally consider at least as fallible as himself, yet he should consider that the unerring eye of God is upon him; and he should endeavor to see that what he does is acceptable in the eye of his Maker and Judge.
entries.79f1132248f6eb8083c9abcc9c286ff793ed445e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24522" type="x-p"/> To do justice and judgment - The words of Samuel to Saul. See note on <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">1Sam 15:23</reference>.
entries.22dd8bc8c365f92071eb76438d91572bde143d43: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24523" type="x-p"/> A high look - The evidence of pride, self-conceit, and vanity. A proud heart, from which the high look, etc., come. <div eID="gen24523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24524" type="x-p"/> And the ploughing - נר ner, lucerna, the lamp, the prosperity and posterity of the wicked; is sin - it is evil in the seed, and evil in the root evil in the branch, and evil in the fruit. They are full of sin themselves, and what they do is sinful.
entries.636b67f9e05ae2c306f05fc29d1e3bdb39223188: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24525" type="x-p"/> Of them that seek death - Instead of מבקשי mebakshey, "them that seek," several MSS., some ancient editions, with Symmachus, the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic, have מקשי mokeshey, the snares. He who gets treasures by a lying tongue, pursues vanity into the snares of death. Our common translation may be as good. But he who, by the snares of his tongue, endeavors to buy and sell to the best advantage, is pursuing what is empty in itself; and he is ensnared by death, while he is attempting to ensnare others.
entries.b8fc20e788909aea447f9059643dc21250bbc026: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24526" type="x-p"/> The robbery of the wicked - The wicked shall be terrified and ruined by the means they use to aggrandize themselves. And as they refuse to do judgment, they shall have judgment without mercy.
entries.ec58167e70ad5a87f1d8c53eab60384d9726d82f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24527" type="x-p"/> In a corner of the housetop - A shed raised on the flat roof - a wide house; בית חבר beith chaber, "a house of fellowship;" what we should call a lodging-house, or a house occupied by several families. This was usual in the East, as well as in the West. Some think a house of festivity is meant: hence my old MS. Bible has, the hous and feste.
entries.3f602dcc308781dcf4e24629bf23243c2dec0113: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24528" type="x-p"/> When the scorner is punished - When those who mock at religion, blaspheme against its Author, and endeavor to poison society, and disturb the peace of the community by their false doctrine, meet with that degree of punishment which their crimes, as far as they affect the public peace, deserve; then the simple, who were either led away, or in danger of being led away, by their pernicious doctrines, are made wise. And when those thus made wise are instructed in the important truths which have been decried by those unprincipled men, then they receive knowledge; and one such public example is made a blessing to thousands. But only blasphemy against God and the Bible should be thus punished. Private opinion the state should not meddle with.
entries.633fe8e4ebf08dfbe7f77ea9d594056ef5cf7c4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24529" type="x-p"/> The righteous man wisely considereth - This verse is understood as implying the pious concern of a righteous man, for a wicked family, whom he endeavors by his instructions to bring into the way of knowledge and peace.
entries.73f21facbbf8e7ee228e132afff7dc1f2bacf769: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24530" type="x-p"/> Whoso stoppeth his ears - See the conduct of the priest and Levite to the man who fell among thieves; and let every man learn from this, that he who shuts his ear against the cry of the poor, shall have the ear of God shut against his cry. The words are quite plain; there is no difficulty here.
entries.4985649ef4c5c61f37e6b4f8447bee3f8ea28ac1: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24531" type="x-p"/> The man once enlightened, that wandereth out of the way of understanding, in which he had walked, shall remain - have a permanent residence - in the congregation of the dead; רפאים rephaim, the lost; either separate spirits in general, or rather the assembly of separate spirits, which had fallen from primitive rectitude; and shall not be restored to the Divine favor; particularly those sinners who were destroyed by the deluge. This passage intimates that those called rephaim are in a state of conscious existence. It is difficult to assign the true meaning of the word in several places where it occurs: but it seems to mean the state of separate spirits, i.e., of those separated from their bodies, and awaiting the judgment of the great day: but the congregation may also include the fallen angels. My old MS. Bible translates, The man that errith fro the wei of doctrine, in the felowschip of geantis schal wonnen.
entries.89c506f52649f5efed8bba43d87b7bca409986f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24532" type="x-p"/> He that loveth pleasure - That follows gaming, fowling, hunting, coursing, etc., when he should be attending to the culture of the fields, shall be a poor man; and, I may safely add, shall be so deservedly poor, as to have none to pity him.
entries.801283e2e10b47e4837895d30392075c0864fa4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24533" type="x-p"/> The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous - God often in his judgments cuts off the wicked, in order to prevent them from destroying the righteous. And in general, we find that the wicked fall into the traps and pits they have digged for the righteous.
entries.2384340f2d32f201fdee35cfb66e0c8d0d4ff3ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24534" type="x-p"/> A wise man scaleth the city of the mighty - Wisdom is in many respects preferable to strength, even in the case of defense. See what skill does in the fortification and reduction of strong places.
entries.8646ea20e970e2b62a5afe68a743075d7757ba3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24535" type="x-p"/> The desire of the slothful killeth him - He desires to eat, drink, and be clothed: but as he does not labor, hence he dies with this desire in his heart, envying those who possess plenty through their labor and industry. Hence he is said to covet greedily all the day long, <reference osisRef="Pro.21.26">Pro 21:26</reference>, while the righteous, who has been laborious and diligent, has enough to eat, and some to spare.
entries.77316837be3342bd0be875eca0007f03cd064bf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24536" type="x-p"/> When he bringeth it with a wicked mind? - If such a person even bring the sacrifices and offerings which God requires, they are an abomination to him, because the man is wicked; and if such offerings be imperfect in themselves, or of goods ill-gotten, or offered by constraint of custom, etc., they are doubly abominable.
entries.c505c2a7c744d3b72b4c9237dad13f795c6e0826: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen24536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24537" type="x-p"/> He directeth his way - Instead of יכין yachin, he directeth, upwards of fifty of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., several ancient editions with some of the versions, read יבין yabin, he understands; and because he understands his way, he is able to direct himself in walking in it.
entries.9e6648987b4e200e5b6e33bb0988a6aa2414832c: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen24537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24538" type="x-p"/> The horse is prepared against the day of battle - Horses were not used among the Jews before the time of Solomon. There was a Divine command against them, <reference osisRef="Deu.17.16">Deu 17:16</reference>; but Solomon transgressed it; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">1Kgs 10:29</reference>. But he here allows that a horse is a vain thing for safety; and that however strong and well appointed cavalry may be, still safety, escape, and victory, are of the Lord. Among the ancient Asiatics, the horse was used only for war; oxen labored in the plough and cart, the ass and the camel carried backloads; and mules and asses served for riding. We often give the credit of a victory to man, when they who consider the circumstances see that it came from God.  <chapter eID="Prov.21"/> <div eID="gen24538" type="x-p"/>

entries.afe4882a554779fb606e758cb18c1f6d397a96c5: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.1">Pro 21:1</reference> <div eID="gen11441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11442" type="x-p"/> The group, like the preceding one, now closes with a proverb of the king. <div eID="gen11442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11443" type="x-p"/> A king's heart in Jahve's hand is like brooks of water; <div eID="gen11443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11444" type="x-p"/> He turneth it whithersoever He will. <div eID="gen11444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11445" type="x-p"/> Brook and canal (the <hi type="italic">Quinta</hi>: ὑδραγωγοί) are both called פּלג, or פּלג, <reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference>, Arab. falaj (from פּלג, to divide, according to which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, διαρέσεις; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. διανομαί; Jerome, <hi type="italic">divisiones</hi>); <hi type="italic">Jâkût</hi> has the explanation of the word: “falaj is the name given to flowing water, particularly the brook from a spring, and every canal which is led from a spring out over flat ground.” Such brooks of water are the heart of a king, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it is compared to such, in Jahve's hand. The second line contains the point of comparison: He inclines it, gives to it the direction (הטּה, causat. of נטה, Num 21:15) toward whatever He will (חפץ denotes willing, as a bending and inclining, viz., of the will; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.2">Pro 18:2</reference>). Rightly Hitzig finds it not accidental that just the expression “brooks of water” is chosen as the figure for tractableness and subjection to government. In <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>, the princes of Judah are compared to “rivers of water in a dry place” with reference to the exhaustion of the land during the oppression of the Assyrian invasion; the proverb has specially in view evidences of kindness proceeding from the heart, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Pro 16:15</reference> the favour of the king is compared to clouds of latter rain emptying themselves in beneficent showers, and at <reference osisRef="Prov.19.12">Pro 19:12</reference> to the dew refreshing the plants. But the speciality of the comparison here is, that the heart of the king, however highly exalted above his subjects, and so removed from their knowledge he may be, has yet One above it by whom it is moved by hidden influences, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the prayer of the oppressed; for man is indeed free, yet he acts under the influence of divinely-directed circumstances and divine operations; and though he reject the guidance of God, yet from his conduct nothing results which the Omniscient, who is surprised by nothing, does not make subservient to His will in the world-plan of redemption. Rightly the Midrash: God gives to the world good or bad kings, according as He seeks to bless it or to visit it with punishment; all decisions that go forth from the king's mouth come לכתחלה, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in their first commencement and their last reason they come from the Holy One.
entries.dd36e08b97677b4d3563cd25c2737c36500bbcfc: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">Pro 21:2</reference> <div eID="gen11445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11446" type="x-p"/> The next group extends from <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">Pro 21:2</reference> to <reference osisRef="Prov.21.8">Pro 21:8</reference>, where it closes as it began. 2 Every way of a man is right in his own eyes;    But a weigher of hearts is Jahve. <div eID="gen11446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11447" type="x-p"/> A proverb similar to <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference> (where דּרכי, for דּרך, זך for ישׁר, רוּחות for לבּות). God is also, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.3">Pro 17:3</reference>, called a trier, בּחן, of hearts, as He is here called a weigher, תּכן. The proverb indirectly admonishes us of the duty of constant self-examination, according to the objective norm of the revealed will of God, and warns us against the self-complacency of the fool, of whom <reference osisRef="Prov.12.15">Pro 12:15</reference> says (as Trimberg in “<hi type="italic">Renner</hi>”): “all fools live in the pleasant feeling that their life is the best,” and against the self-deception which walks in the way of death and dreams of walking in the way of life, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.12">Pro 14:12</reference> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.25">Pro 16:25</reference>).
entries.0d508fd6d402ac3fa4122f137ed34d8d48147b0c: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.3">Pro 21:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.3">3</reference> To practice justice and right    Hath with Jahve the pre-eminence above sacrifice. <div eID="gen11447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11448" type="x-p"/> We have already (vol. i. p. 42) shown how greatly this depreciation of the works of the ceremonial <hi type="italic">cultus</hi>, as compared with the duties of moral obedience, is in the spirit of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>; cf. also at Pro 15:8. Prophecy also gives its testimony, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Hos 6:7, according to which also here (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.20.8">Pro 20:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">Isa 9:8</reference>) the practising of צדקה וּמשׁפּט (sequence of words as at <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.5">Psa 33:5</reference>, elsewhere צדק ומשׁפט, and yet more commonly משׁפט וצדקה) does not denote legal rigour, but the practising of the <hi type="italic">justum et aequum</hi>, or much rather the <hi type="italic">aequum et bonum</hi>, thus in its foundation conduct proceeding from the principle of love. The <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. עשׂה (like קנה, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.16">Pro 16:16</reference>) occurs three times (here and at <reference osisRef="Gen.50.20">Gen 50:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">Psa 101:3</reference>); once עשׂו is written (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.18">Gen 31:18</reference>), as also in the <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>. the form עשׂה mro and עשׂו interchange (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Norzi at <reference osisRef="Jer.22.4">Jer 22:4</reference>); once עשׂהוּ for עשׂותו (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.18">Exo 18:18</reference>) occurs in the <hi type="italic">status conjunctus</hi>.
entries.98d9b8f2aa26415cb4bcd4d310ef74df3c8ab955: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.4">Pro 21:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.4">4</reference> Loftiness of eyes and swelling of heart -    The husbandry of the godless is sin. <div eID="gen11448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11449" type="x-p"/> If נר, in the sense of light, gives a satisfactory meaning, then one might appeal to 1Ki 11:36 (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:17</reference>), where ניר appears to signify lamp, in which meaning it is once (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.29">2Sa 22:29</reference>) written ניר (like חיק); or since ניר = נר (ground-form, nawir, lightening) is as yet certainly established neither in the Heb. nor Syr., one might punctuate נר instead of נר, according to which the Greeks, Aram., and Luther, with Jerome, translate. But of the lamp of the godless we read at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.9">Pro 13:9</reference> and elsewhere, that it goeth out. We must here understand by נר the brilliant prosperity (Bertheau and others) of the wicked, or their “proud spirit flaming and flaring like a bright light” (Zöckler), which is contrary to the use of the metaphor as found elsewhere, which does not extend to a prosperous condition. We must then try another meaning for נר; but not that of yoke, for this is not Heb., but Aram.-Arab., and the interpretation thence derived by Lagarde: “Haughtiness and pride; but the godless for all that bear their yoke, viz., sin,” seeks in vain to hide behind the “for all that” the breaking asunder of the two lines of the verse. In Heb. נר means that which lightens (burning) = lamp, נוּר, the shining (that which burns) = fire, and ניר, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.23">Pro 13:23</reference>, from ניר, to plough up (Targ. <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.12">1Sa 8:12</reference>, למנר = לחרשׁ) the fresh land, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the breaking up of the fallow land; according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. as Kimchi: νέωμα ἀσεβῶν ἁμαρτία, which as Ewald and Elster explain: “where a disposition of wicked haughtiness, of unbridled pride, prevails, there will also sin be the first-fruit on the field of action; נר, <hi type="italic">novale</hi>, the field turned up for the first time, denotes here the first-fruits of sin.” But why just the first-fruits, and not the fruit in general? We are better to abide by the field itself, which is here styled נר, not שׂדה (or as once in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.10">Jer 39:10</reference>, יגב); because with this word, more even than with שׂדה, is connected the idea of agricultural work, of arable land gained by the digging up or the breaking up of one or more years' fallow ground (cf. Pea ii. 1, ניר, Arab. siḳâḳ, opp. בור, Arab. bûr, <hi type="italic">Menachoth</hi> 85a, שׂדות מניּרות, a fresh broken-up field, Erachin 29b, נר ,, opp. הביר, to let lie fallow), so that נר רשׁעים may mean the cultivation of the fields, and generally the husbandry, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the whole conduct and life of the godless. נר is here ethically metaph., but not like Hos 10:12; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.3">Jer 4:3</reference>, where it means a new moral commencement of life; but like חרשׁ, <hi type="italic">arare</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; Hos 10:13; cf. Pro 3:29. רחב is not adj. like <reference osisRef="Prov.28.25">Pro 28:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>, but infin. like חסר, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pro 10:21</reference>; and accordingly also רוּם is not adj. like חוּם, or past like סוּג, but infin. like Isa 10:12. And חטּאת is the pred. of the complex subject, which consists of רוּם עינים, a haughty looking down with the eyes, רחב־לב, breadth of heart, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, excess of self-consciousness, and נר רשׁעים taken as an <hi type="italic">asyndeton summativum</hi>: pride of look, and making oneself large of heart, in short, the whole husbandry of the godless, or the whole of the field cultivated by them, with all that grows thereon, is sin.
entries.ce96e27e28d6ff09c39399286172bd738b483804: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.5">Pro 21:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.5">5</reference> The striving of the diligent is only to advantage.    And hastening all [excessive haste] only to loss; or in other words, and agreeably to the Heb. construction: <div eID="gen11449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11450" type="x-p"/> The thoughts of the industrious are (reach) only to gain, <div eID="gen11450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11451" type="x-p"/> And every one who hastens - it (this his hastening) is only to loss. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., at Pro 17:21. At <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>, Luther translates “the hand of the diligent,” here “the plans of an expert [<hi type="italic">endelichen</hi>],” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of one actively striving (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.29">Pro 22:29</reference>, <hi type="italic">endelich</hi> = מהיר) to the end. The אץ, hastening overmuch, is contrasted with the diligent: Luther well: but he who is altogether too precipitant. Everywhere else in the Proverbs אץ has a closer definition with it, wherefore Hitzig reads אצר, which must mean: he who collects together; but אץ along with חרוץ is perfectly distinct. The thought is the same as our “<hi type="italic">eile mit Weile</hi>” [= <hi type="italic">festina lente</hi>], and Goethe's <div eID="gen11451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11452" type="x-p"/> Wie das Gestirn ohne Hast, <div eID="gen11452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11453" type="x-p"/> Aber ohne Rast <div eID="gen11453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11454" type="x-p"/> Drehe sich jeder <div eID="gen11454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11455" type="x-p"/> Um die eigne Last. “Like the stars, without haste but without rest, let every one carry about his own burden,” viz., of his calling that lies upon him. The fundamental meaning of אוץ is to throng, to urge (<reference osisRef="Exod.5.13">Exo 5:13</reference>), here of impatient and inconsiderate rashness. While on the side of the diligent there is nothing but gain, such haste brings only loss; over-exertion does injury, and the work will want care, circumspection, and thoroughness. In the Book of Proverbs, the contrasts “gain” and “loss” frequently occur, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pro 11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.23">Pro 14:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.16">Pro 22:16</reference> : profit (the increase of capital by interest), opp. loss (of capital, or of part thereof), as commercial terms.
entries.1c4b294edb21cdd8f679705cc1ade98c654391ea: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.6">Pro 21:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.6">6</reference> The gaining of treasures by a lying tongue    Is a fleeting breath of such as seek death. <div eID="gen11455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11456" type="x-p"/> One may, at any rate, after the free manner of gnomic resemblances and comparisons, regard “fleeting breath” and “such as seek death” as two separated predicates: such gain is fleeting breath, so those who gain are seeking death (Caspari's <hi type="italic">Beiträge zu Jes</hi>. p. 53). But it is also syntactically admissible to interpret the words rendered “seekers of death” as gen.; for such interruptions of the <hi type="italic">st. constr</hi>., as here by נדּף [fleeting], frequently occur, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.13">1Ch 9:13</reference>; and that an idea, in spite of such interruption, may be thought of as gen., is seen from the Arab.<note placement="foot">Note: <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Friedr. Philippi's <hi type="italic">Status constructus</hi>, p. 17, Anm. 3; and cf. therewith such constructions as (Arab.) mân'u faḍlah âlmanhtâji, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a refuser of the needy, his beneficence = one who denies to the needy his beneficence.</note> <div eID="gen11456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11457" type="x-p"/> But the text is unsettled. Symmachus, Syr., Targ., the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther render the phrase מבקשׁי [seekers]; but the lxx and Jerome read מוקשׁי [snares] (cf. <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">1Ti 6:9</reference>); this word Rashi also had before him (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Norzi), and Kennicott found it in several Codd. Bertheau prefers it, for he translates: ...is fleeting breath, snares of death; Ewald and Hitzig go further, for, after the lxx, they change the whole proverb into: מות (בּמוקשׁי) הבל רדף אל־מוקשׁי, with פּעל in the first line. But διώκει of the lxx is an incorrect rendering of נדף, which the smuggling in of the ἐπὶ (παγίδας θανάτου) drew after it, without our concluding therefrom that אל־מוקשׁי, or למוקשׁי (Lagarde), lay before the translators; on the contrary, the word which (Cappellus) lay before them, מוקשׁי, certainly deserves to be preferred to מבקשׁי: the possession is first, in view of him who has gotten it, compared to a fleeting (נדּף, as <reference osisRef="Isa.42.2">Isa 42:2</reference>) breath (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, smoke, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.3">Psa 68:3</reference>), and then, in view of the inheritance itself and its consequences, is compared to the snares of death (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.14">Pro 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.27">Pro 14:27</reference>); for in פּעל (here equivalent to עשׂות, <hi type="italic">acquisitio</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.1">Gen 31:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">Deu 8:17</reference>) lie together the ideas of him who procures and of the thing that is procured or effected (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.11">Pro 20:11</reference>).
entries.075d814c7454a84481c892cf130cf800f5f91436: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.7">Pro 21:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.7">7</reference> The violence of the godless teareth them away,    For they have refused to do what is right. <div eID="gen11457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11458" type="x-p"/> The destruction which they prepare for others teareth or draggeth them away to destruction, by which wicked conduct brings punishment on itself; their own conduct is its own executioner (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.19">Pro 1:19</reference>); for refusing to practise what is right, they have pronounced judgment against themselves, and fallen under condemnation. Rightly Jerome, <hi type="italic">detrahent</hi>, with Aquila, κατασπάσει = j'gurrem (as <reference osisRef="Hab.1.15">Hab 1:15</reference>), from גּרר; on the contrary, the lxx incorrectly, ἐπιξενωθήσεται, from גוּר, to dwell, to live as a guest; and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., as Luther, in opposition to the <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>.: δεδίξεται (fut. of δεδίσσεσθαι, to terrify), from גוּר, to dread, fear, which also remains intrans., with the accus. following, Deu 32:27. The Syr. and the Targ. freely: robbery (Targ. רבּוּנא, perhaps in the sense of usury) will seize them, viz., in the way of punishment. In Arab. jarr (jariyratn) means directly to commit a crime; not, as Schultens explains, <hi type="italic">admittere crimen paenam trahens</hi>, but <hi type="italic">attrahere</hi> (<hi type="italic">arripere</hi>), like (Arab.) jany (jinâytn), <hi type="italic">contrahere crimen</hi>; for there the crime is thought of as violent usurpation, here as wicked accumulation.
entries.3a7834ad147abf132818c37bd2338298052321fc: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.8">Pro 21:8</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.8">8</reference> Winding is the way of a man laden with guilt;    But the pure - his conduct is right. <div eID="gen11458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11459" type="x-p"/> Rightly the accentuation places together “the way of a man” as subject, and “winding” as predicate: if the poet had wished to say (Schultens, Bertheau) “one crooked in his way” (<hi type="italic">quoad viam</hi>), he would have contented himself with the phrase נחפּך דּרך. But, on the other hand, the accentuation is scarcely correct (the second <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> is a transformed <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>), for it interprets וזר as a second pred.; but וזר is adj. to אישׁ. As הפכפּך (synon. פּתלתּל, עקלקל) is a <hi type="italic">hapax leg</hi>., so also vazar, which is equivalent to (Arab.) mawzwr, <hi type="italic">crimine onustus</hi>, from wazria, <hi type="italic">crimen committere</hi>, properly to charge oneself with a crime. The ancient interpreters have, indeed, no apprehension of this meaning before them; the lxx obtain from the proverb a thought reminding us of <reference osisRef="Ps.18.27">Psa 18:27</reference>, in which vazar does not at all appear; the Syr. and Targ. translate as if the <hi type="italic">vav</hi> of vazar introduces the conclusion: he is a barbarian (<hi type="italic">nuchrojo</hi>); Luther: he is crooked; Jerome also sets aside the syntax: <hi type="italic">perversa via viri aliena est</hi>; but, syntactically admissible, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. and Kimchi, as the Jewish interpreters generally, διαστροφωτάτη ὁδὸς ἀνδρὸς καὶ ἀλλόκοτος. Fleischer here even renounces the help of the Arab., for he translates: <hi type="italic">Tortuosa est via viri criminibus onusti, qui autem sancte vivit, is recte facit</hi>; but he adds thereto the remark that “vazar thus explained, with Cappellus, Schultens, and Gesenius, would, it is true, corresponding to the Arab. wazar, have first the abstract meaning of a verbal noun from wazira;<note placement="foot">Note: The <hi type="italic">n. act</hi> formed from wazara is wazr, wizr, wizat. These three forms would correspond to the Heb. vězěr, vēzěr, and zěrěth (z'rāh, cf. rěděth, r'dah, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.3">Gen 46:3</reference>).</note> the old explanation is therefore perhaps better: <hi type="italic">tortuosa est via viri et deflectens</hi> (<hi type="italic">scil. a recta linea</hi>, thus <hi type="italic">devia est</hi>), when the '<hi type="italic">viri</hi>' is to be taken in the general sense of 'many, this and that one;' the closer definition is reflected from the זך of the second clause.” But (1) זר as an adj. signifies <hi type="italic">peregrinus</hi>; one ought thus rather to expect סר, degenerated, corrupt, although that also does not rightly accord; (2) the verbal noun also, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, 'all, passes over into a subst. and adj. signification (the latter without distinction of number and gender); (3) וזר, after its adj. signification, is related to (Arab.) wazyr, as חכם is to ḥakym, רזב to rahyb; it is of the same form as ענו, with which it has in common its derivation from a root of similar meaning, and its ethical signification. In 8b, וזך is rightly accented as subj. of the complex pred. זך is the pure in heart and of a good conscience. The laden with guilt (guilty) strikes out all kinds of crooked ways; but the pure needs not stealthy ways, he does not stand under the pressure of the bondage of sin, the ban of the guilt of sin; his conduct is straightforward, directed by the will of God, and not by cunning policy. Schultens: <hi type="italic">Integer vitae scelerisque purus non habet cur vacillet, cur titubet, cur sese contorqueat</hi>. The choice of the designation וזך [and the pure] may be occasioned by וזר (Hitzig); the expression 8b reminds us of Pro 20:11.
entries.7e12128671ec28056dd9d7e6b5d8f0fb19b8a5bd: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.9">Pro 21:9</reference> <div eID="gen11459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11460" type="x-p"/> The group now following extends to <reference osisRef="Prov.21.18">Pro 21:18</reference>, where a new one begins with a variation of its initial verse. 9 Better to sit on the pinnacle of a house-roof,    Than a contentious wife and a house in common. <div eID="gen11460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11461" type="x-p"/> We have neither to supplement the second line: than with a contentious wife... (Symmachus, Theodotion, Jerome, Luther), nor: than that one have a contentious...; but the meaning is, that sitting on the roof-top better befits one, does better than a quarrelsome wife and a common house (rightly the Targ. and <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in a common house; for the connecting together of the wife and the house by <hi type="italic">vav</hi> is a Semitic <hi type="italic">hendiadys</hi>, a juxtaposition of two ideas which our language would place in a relation of subordination (Fleischer). This <hi type="italic">hendiadys</hi> would, indeed, be scarcely possible if the idea of the married wife were attached to אושׁת; for that such an one has with her husband a “house of companionship, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a common house,” is self-evident. But may it not with equal right be understood of the imperious positive mother-in-law of a widower, a splenetic shrewish aunt, a sickly female neighbour disputing with all the world, and the like? A man must live together with his wife in so far as he does not divorce her; he must then escape from her; but a man may also be constrained by circumstances to live in a house with a quarrelsome mother-in-law, and such an one may, even during the life of his wife, and in spite of her affection, make his life so bitter that he would rather, in order that he might have rest, sit on the pinnacle or ridge of a house-roof. פּנּהּ is the battlement (Zep 1:16) of the roof, the edge of the roof, or its summit; he who sits there does so not without danger, and is exposed to the storm, but that in contrast with the alternative is even to be preferred; he sits alone. Regarding the Chethı̂b מדינים, Kerı̂ מדינים, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.6.14">Pro 6:14</reference>; and cf. the figures of the “continual dropping” for the continual scolding of such a wife, embittering the life of her husband, Pro 19:13.
entries.a894bc51602ada2e9c54c273036ff3af0cc82aaa: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.10">Pro 21:10</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.10">10</reference> The soul of the godless hath its desire after evil;      His neighbour findeth no mercy in his eyes. <div eID="gen11461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11462" type="x-p"/> The interchange of perf. and fut. cannot be without intention. Löwenstein renders the former as <hi type="italic">perf. hypotheticum</hi>: if the soul of the wicked desires anything evil...; but the רשׁע wishes evil not merely now and then, but that is in general his nature and tendency. The perf. expresses that which is actually the case: the soul of the wicked has its desire directed (write אוּתה with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, after Codd. and old Ed., not with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>) toward evil, and the fut. expresses that which proceeds from this: he who stands near him is not spared. יחן is, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Isa 26:10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Hoph</hi>. of חנן, to incline, viz., oneself, compassionately toward any one, or to bend to him. But in what sense is בּעיניו added? It does not mean, as frequently, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">Pro 21:2</reference>, according to his judgment, nor, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.8">Pro 20:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.13">Pro 6:13</reference> : with his eyes, but is to be understood after the phrase מצא חן בּעיני: his neighbour finds no mercy in his eyes, so that in these words the sympathy ruling within him expresses itself: “his eyes will not spare his friends,” <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Isa 13:18.
entries.69124ec696218abe709df73a78fd226549e98a6f: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.11">Pro 21:11</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.11">11</reference> When the scorner is punished, the simple is made wise;      And when insight is imparted to a wise man, he receives knowledge. <div eID="gen11462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11463" type="x-p"/> The thought is the same as at Pro 19:25. The mocker at religion and virtue is incorrigible, punishment avails him nothing, but yet it is not lost; for as a warning example it teaches the simple, who might otherwise be easily drawn into the same frivolity. On the other hand, the wise man needs no punishment, but only strengthening and furtherance: if “instruction” is imparted to him, he embraces it, makes it his own דּעת; for, being accessible to better insight, he gains more and more knowledge. De Dieu, Bertheau, and Zöckler make “the simple” the subject also in 11b: and if a wise man prospers, he (the simple) gains knowledge. But השׂכּיל ל, used thus impersonally, is unheard of; wherefore Hitzig erases the ל before חכם erofeb ל eh: if a wise man has prosperity. But השׂכיל does not properly mean to have prosperity, but only mediately: to act with insight, and on that account with success. The thought that the simple, on the one side, by the merited punishment of the mocker; on the other, by the intelligent prosperous conduct of the wise, comes to reflection, to reason, may indeed be entertained, but the traditional form of the proverb does not need any correction. השׂכּיל may be used not only transitively: to gain insight, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.6">Gen 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">Psa 2:10</reference>, and elsewhere, but also causatively: to make intelligent, with the accus. following, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.23">Pro 16:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>, or: to offer, present insight, as here with the dat.-obj. following (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">Pro 17:26</reference>). Instead of בּענשׁ־, the <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> of which is false, Codd. and good Edd. have, rightly, בּענשׁ־. Hitzig, making “the wise” the subject to בהשׂכיל (and accordingly “the scorner” would be the subject in 11a), as a correct consequence reads בּענשׁ = בּהענשׁ. For us, with that first correction, this second one also fails. “Both <hi type="italic">infinitivi constr</hi>.,” Fleischer remarks, “are to be taken passively; for the Semitic infin., even of transitive form, as it has no designation of gender, time, and person, is an indeterminate <hi type="italic">modus</hi>, even in regard to the <hi type="italic">generis verbi</hi> (Act. and Pass.).”<note placement="foot">Note: The Arab. National Grammarians, it is true, view the matter otherwise. When ḳatlu zydn, the putting to death of Zeid, is used in the sense of Zeid's becoming dead, according to their view the fâ'l (the <hi type="italic">gen. subjecti</hi>) is omitted; the full expression would be ḳatlu 'amrn zaydnâ. Since now 'amrn is omitted, zaydn has in the gen. form taken the place of the fâ'l, but this gen. is the representative of the <hi type="italic">acc. objecti</hi>. Without thus going round about, we say: it is the <hi type="italic">gen. objecti</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen11463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11464" type="x-p"/> To this proverb with u-behaskil there is connected the one that follows, beginning with <hi type="italic">maskil</hi>.
entries.0e40efb2c77df7a15727031c661cb38537faf48a: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.12">Pro 21:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.12">12</reference> A righteous One marketh the house of the godless;      He hurleth the godless to destruction. <div eID="gen11464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11465" type="x-p"/> If we understand by the word צדּיק a righteous man, then 12a would introduce the warning which he gives, and the unexpressed subject of 12b must be God (Umbreit). But after such an <hi type="italic">introitus</hi>, יהוה ought not to be wanting. If in 12a “the righteous man” is the subject, then it presents itself as such also for the second parallel part. But the thought that the righteous, when he takes notice of the house of the godless, shows attention which of itself hurls the godless into destruction (Löwenstein), would require the sing. רשׁע in the conclusion; also, instead of מסלּף the fut. יסלּף would have been found; and besides, the judicial סלּף (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding this word at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.3">Pro 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Pro 19:3</reference>) would not be a suitable word for this confirmation in evil. Thus by צדיק the proverb means God, and מסלף has, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.22.12">Pro 22:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.19">Job 12:19</reference>, this word as its subject. “A righteous One” refers to the All-righteous, who is called, <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference>, “the All-just One,” and by Rashi, under the passage before us, צדּיקו שׁל־עולם. Only do not translate with Bertheau and Zöckler: the Righteous One (All-righteous), for (1) this would require הצּדּיק, and (2) הצדיק is never by itself used as an attributive designation of God. Rightly, Fleischer and Ewald: a Righteous One, viz., God. It is the indetermination which seeks to present the idea of the great and dreadful: a Righteous One, and such a Righteous One!<note placement="foot">Note: The Arabs call this indetermination âlnkrt lalt'ẓym wallthwyl. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., under Psa 2:12.</note> השׂכיל with על, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.20">Pro 16:20</reference>, or אל, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.2">Psa 41:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.8.13">Neh 8:13</reference>, here with ל, signifies to give attention to anything, to look attentively on it. The two participles stand in the same line: <hi type="italic">animum advertit</hi> ... <hi type="italic">evertit</hi>. Hitzig changes לבּית רשׁע into לבּיתו, and makes רשׁע the subject of 12b; but the proverb as it lies before us is far more intelligible.
entries.488b7a8371b4f860665dc197ba0e656a06b8378a: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.13">Pro 21:13</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.13">13</reference> He that stoppeth his ear at the cry of the poor      he also calls and is not heard. <div eID="gen11465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11466" type="x-p"/> Only the merciful find mercy, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.7">Mat 5:7</reference>; the unmerciful rich man, who has no ear for the cry of the דל, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of him who is without support and means of subsistence, thus of one who is needing support, will also remain unheard when he himself, in the time of need, calls upon God for help. Cf. the parable of the unmerciful servant of the merciful king, Mat 18:23. מן in מזּעקת, as <reference osisRef="Isa.23.15">Isa 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.13">Gen 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.27.1">Gen 27:1</reference>; no preposition of our [German] language [nor English] expresses, as Fleischer here remarks, such a fulness of meaning as this מן does, to which, after a verb of shutting up such as אטם (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.28">Pro 17:28</reference>), the Arab. 'n would correspond, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, â'my 'n âltryḳ: blind, so that he does not see the way.
entries.af06fabf94a42c43934f7c907661808c42b0a963: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.14">Pro 21:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.14">14</reference> A gift in secret turneth away anger;      And a bribe into the bosom violent wrath. <div eID="gen11466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11467" type="x-p"/> Hitzig reads with Symmachus, the Targ., and Jerome, יכבּה, and translates: “extinguishes anger;” but it does not follow that they did read יכבה; for the Talm. Heb. כּפה signifies to cover by turning over, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, of a vessel, Sanhedrin 77a, which, when it is done to a candle or a fire, may mean its extinction. But כפה of the post-bibl. Heb. also means to bend, and thence to force out (Aram. כּפא, כּפי), according to which Kimchi hesitates whether to explain: overturns = smothers, or: bends = forces down anger. The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. follows the latter signification: κάμψει (for Villoison's καλύψει rests on a false reading of the MS). But there is yet possible another derivation from the primary signification, <hi type="italic">curvare, flectere, vertere</hi>, according to which the lxx translates ἀνατρέπει, for which ἀποτρέπει would be yet better: כפה, to bend away, to turn off, ἀρκεῖν, <hi type="italic">arcere</hi>, altogether like the Arab. (compared by Schultens) kfâ, and kfy, ἀρκεῖν, to prevent, whence, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, ikfı̂ni hada: hold that away from me, or: spare me that (Fleischer); with the words hafı̂ka sharran (Lat. <hi type="italic">defendaris semper a malo</hi>) princes were anciently saluted; kfy signifies “to suffice,” because enough is there, where there is a keeping off of want. Accordingly we translate: <hi type="italic">Donum clam acceptum avertit iram</hi>, which also the Syr. meant by mephadka (מפרק). This verb is naturally to be supplied to 14b, which the lxx has recognised (it translates: but he who spares gifts, excites violent anger). Regarding שׂחד, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">Pro 17:8</reference>; and regarding בּחק, at Pro 17:23. Also here חק (חיק = חיק), like Arab. jayb, 'ubb, חב, denotes the bosom of the garment; on the contrary (Arab.) hijr, hiḍn, חצן, is more used of that of the body, or that formed by the drawing together of the body (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, of the arm in carrying a child). A present is meant which one brings with him concealed in his bosom; perhaps 13b called to mind the judge that took gifts, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.8">Exo 23:8</reference> (Hitzig).
entries.ef00eac0924306f1c6873446cc39d344a1aae991: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.15">Pro 21:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.15">15</reference> It is a joy to the just to do justice,      And a terror for them that work iniquity. <div eID="gen11467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11468" type="x-p"/> To act according to the law of rectitude is to these as unto death; injustice has become to them a second nature, so that their heart strives against rectitude of conduct; it also enters to little into their plan of life, and their economy, that they are afraid of ruining themselves thereby. So we believe, with Hitzig, Elster, Zöckler, and Luther, this must be explained in accordance with our interpretation of Pro 10:29. Fleischer and others supplement the second parallel member from the first: וּפעל און מחתּה לפעלי אין; others render 15b as an independent sentence: ruin falls on those who act wickedly. But that ellipsis is hard and scarcely possible; but in general מחתה, as contrasted correlate to שׂמחה, can scarcely have the pure objective sense of ruin or destruction. It must mean a revolution in the heart. Right-doing is to the righteous a pleasure (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.23">Pro 10:23</reference>); and for those who have און, and are devoid of moral worth, and thus simply immoral as to the aim and sphere of their conduct, right-doing is something which alarms them: when they act in conformity with what is right, they do so after an external impulse only against their will, as if it were death to them.
entries.cfdc92197eb4a36d006ab410c244c70a0166a7c0: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.16">Pro 21:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.16">16</reference> A man who wanders from the way of understanding,      Shall dwell in the assembly of the dead. <div eID="gen11468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11469" type="x-p"/> Regarding השׂכּל, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.3">Pro 1:3</reference>; and regarding רפאים, Pro 2:18. The verb נוּח means to repose, to take rest, <reference osisRef="Job.3.13">Job 3:13</reference>, and to dwell anywhere, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.33">Pro 14:33</reference>; but originally like (Arab.) nâkh and hadd, to lay oneself down anywhere, and there to come to rest; and that is the idea which is here connected with ינוּח, for the figurative description of יאבד or ימוּת is formed after the designation of the subject, 16a: he who, forsaking the way of understanding, walks in the way of error, at length comes to the assembly of the dead; for every motion has an end, and every journey a goal, whether it be one that is self-appointed or which is appointed for him. Here also it is intimated that the way of the soul which loves wisdom and follows her goes in another direction than earthwards down into hades; hades and death, its background appear here as punishments, and it is true that as such one may escape them.
entries.0815967e042ee57a7f7a1f08db66d35ee8c8d94e: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.17">Pro 21:17</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.17">17</reference> He who loveth pleasure becometh a man of want;      He who loveth wine and oil doth not become rich. <div eID="gen11469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11470" type="x-p"/> In Arab. samh denotes the joyful action of the “cheerful giver,” <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2Co 9:7</reference>; in Heb. the joyful affection; here, like farah, pleasure, delight, festival of joy. Jerome: <hi type="italic">qui diligit epulas</hi>. For feasting is specially thought of, where wine was drunk, and oil and other fragrant essences were poured (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.27.9">Pro 27:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amo 6:6</reference>) on the head and the clothes. He who loves such festivals, and is commonly found there, becomes a man of want, or suffers want (cf. Jdg 12:2, אישׁ ריב, a man of strife); such an one does not become rich (העשׁיר, like <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>, = עשׂה עשׁר, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.11">Jer 17:11</reference>); he does not advance, and thus goes backwards.
entries.d3c63a91c38032c6d1f09f5359629880d2a08f75: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.18">Pro 21:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.18">18</reference> The godless becometh a ransom for the righteous;      And the faithless cometh into the place of the upright. <div eID="gen11470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11471" type="x-p"/> The thought is the same as at Pro 11:8. An example of this is, that the same world-commotion which brought the nations round Babylon for its destruction, put an end to Israel's exile: Cyrus, the instrument in God's hands for inflicting punishment on many heathen nations, was Israel's liberator, Isa 43:3. Another example is in the exchange of places by Haman and Mordecai, to which Rashi refers. כּפר is equivalent to λύτρον, ransom; but it properly signifies price of atonement, and generally, means of reconciliation, which covers or atones for the guilt of any one; the poll-tax and “oblations” also, Exo 30:15., Num 31:50, are placed under this point of view, as blotting out guilt: if the righteousness of God obtains satisfaction, it makes its demand against the godless, and lets the righteous go free; or, as the substantival clause 18b expresses, the faithless steps into the place of the upright, for the wrath passes by the latter and falls upon the former. Regarding בּוגד, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 2:22. Thus, in contrast to the ישׁר, he is designated, who keeps faith neither with God nor man, and with evil intention enters on deceitful ways - the faithless, the malicious, the assassin.
entries.cd748196914d095bb6bba088bf2903431b7df5bf: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.19">Pro 21:19</reference> <div eID="gen11471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11472" type="x-p"/> With this verse, a doublet to <reference osisRef="Prov.21.9">Pro 21:9</reference> (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.24">Pro 25:24</reference>), the collector makes a new addition; in <reference osisRef="Prov.21.29">Pro 21:29</reference> he reaches a proverb which resembles the closing proverb of the preceding group, in its placing in contrast the רשׁע and ישׁר; - <div eID="gen11472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11473" type="x-p"/> It is better to dwell in a waste land, <div eID="gen11473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11474" type="x-p"/> Than a contentious wife and vexation. <div eID="gen11474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11475" type="x-p"/> The corner of the roof, Hitzig remarks, has been made use of, and the author must look further out for a lonely seat. But this is as piquant as it is devoid of thought; for have both proverbs the same author, and if so, were they coined at the same time? Here also it is unnecessary to regard מאשׁת as an abbreviation for משּׁבת עם אשׁת. Hitzig supplies שׁכן, by which אשׁת, as the accus.-obj., is governed; but it is not to be supplied, for the proverb places as opposite to one another dwelling in a waste land (read שׁבת בּארץ־מדבּר, with Codd. and correct Ed.) and a contentious wife (Chethı̂b, מדונים, Kerı̂, מדינים) and vexation, and says the former is better than the latter. For וכעס [and vexation] is not, as translated by the ancients, and generally received, a second governed genitive to אשׁת, but dependent on מן, follows “contentious woman” (cf. 9b): better that than a quarrelsome wife, and at the same time vexation.
entries.0a8ba67f1f4238fd176cb204ba200d7eb181da15: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.20">Pro 21:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.20">20</reference> Precious treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the wise;      And a fool of a man squanders it. <div eID="gen11475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11476" type="x-p"/> The wise spares, the fool squanders; and if the latter enters on the inheritance which the former with trouble and care collected, it is soon devoured. The combination אוצר נחמד ושׁמן [desirable treasure and oil] has something inconcinnate, wherefore the accentuation places אוצר by itself by <hi type="italic">Mehuppach Legarmeh</hi>; but it is not to be translated “a treasure of that which is precious, and oil,” since it is punctuated אוצר, and not אוצר; and besides, in that case מחמדּים would have been used instead of נחמד. Thus by אוצר נחמד, a desirable and splendid capital in gold and things of value (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.19.11">Psa 19:11</reference>); and by שׁמן, mentioned by way of example, stores in kitchen and cellar are to be thought of, which serve him who lives luxuriously, and afford noble hospitality, - a fool of a man (כּסיל אדם, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20">Pro 15:20</reference>), who finds this, devours it, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, quickly goes through it, makes, in short, a <hi type="italic">tabula rasa</hi> of it; cf. בּלע, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Isa 28:4</reference>, with בּלּע, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.26">2Sa 20:26</reference>, and Pro 19:28. The suffix of יבלּענּוּ refers back to אוצר as the main idea, or distributively also both to the treasure and the oil. The lxx (θησαυρὸς ἐπιθυμητὸς) ἀναπαύσεται ἐπὶ στόματος σοφοῦ, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, ישׁכן בפה חכם, according to which Hitzig corrects; but the fool, he who swallows down “the precious treasure with a wise mouth,” is a being we can scarcely conceive of. His taste is not at all bad; why then a fool? Is it perhaps because he takes more in than he can at one time digest? The reading of the lxx is corrected by 20b.
entries.d80398045e43e2308ea5b22e31ee7a6a21537c9b: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.21">Pro 21:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.21">21</reference> He that followeth after righteousness and kindness      Will obtain life, righteousness, and honour. <div eID="gen11476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11477" type="x-p"/> How we are to render צדקה וחסד is seen from the connection of <reference osisRef="Prov.21.3">Pro 21:3</reference> and Hos 6:7 : tsedakah is conduct proceeding from the principle of self-denying and compassionate love, which is the essence of the law, Mic 6:8; and hesed is conduct proceeding from sympathy, which, placing itself in the room of another, perceives what will benefit him, and sets about doing it (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference> : to him who is inwardly melted disheartened חסד is due from his neighbour). The reward which one who strives thus to act obtains, is designated 21b by חיּים and כּבוד. Honour and life stand together, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.4">Pro 22:4</reference>, when עשׁר precedes, and here צדקה stands between, which, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.18">Pro 8:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference>, is thought of as that which is distributed as a gift of heaven, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>, which has glory in its train, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.8">Isa 58:8</reference>; as Paul also says, “Whom He justified, them He also glorified.” The lxx has omitted tsedakah, because it can easily appear as erroneously repeated from 21a. But in reality there are three good things which are promised to those who are zealous in the works of love: a prosperous life, enduring righteousness, true honour. Life as it proceeds from God, the Living One, righteousness as it avails the righteous and those doing righteously before God, honour or glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference>) as it is given (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.12">Psa 84:12</reference>) by the God of glory. Cf. with חיים צדקה, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">Pro 10:2</reference>, and with צדקה, especially Jam 2:13, κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως.
entries.d5738b6061007a7892c5e7e3609720c6a43eb61b: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pro 21:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">22</reference> A wise man scaleth a city of the mighty;      And casteth down the fortress in which they trusted. <div eID="gen11477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11478" type="x-p"/> Ecc 9:14. is a side-piece to this, according to which a single wise man, although poor, may become the deliverer of a city besieged by a great army, and destitute of the means of defence. עלה, <hi type="italic">seq. acc</hi>., means to climb up, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.7">Joe 2:7</reference>; here, of the scaling of a fortified town, viz., its fortress. עז is that which makes it עיר עז, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Isa 26:1</reference> : its armour of protection, which is designated by the genit. מבטחה, as the object and ground of their confidence. The vocalization מבטחה, for mibtachcha (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13">Jer 48:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="Job.18.14">Job 18:14</reference>), follows the rule Gesen. §27, Anm. 2b. The suff., as in לאתננּה, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">Isa 23:17</reference>, is lightened, because if its <hi type="italic">mappik</hi>, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 30b; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding the various grounds of these <hi type="italic">formae raphatae pro mappicatis</hi>, Böttcher, §418. If a city is defended by ever so many valiant men, the wise man knows the point where it may be overcome, and knows how to organize the assault so as to destroy the proud fortress. With ויּרד, he brings to ruin, cf. עד רדתּהּ, Deu 20:20.
entries.c6bce60dabd40476acf1965276868b32bb30a4b0: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.23">Pro 21:23</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.23">23</reference> He that guardeth his mouth and his tongue,      Keepeth his soul from troubles. <div eID="gen11478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11479" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Prov.13.3">Pro 13:3</reference> resembles this. He guardeth his mouth who does not speak when he does better to be silent; and he guardeth his tongue who says no more than is right and fitting. The troubles comprehend both external and internal evils, hurtful incidents and (נפשׁ) צרות לבב, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">Psa 25:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Psa 31:8</reference>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, distress of conscience, self-accusation, sorrow on account of the irreparable evil which one occasions.
entries.a3b928f703ad9abe07ad23652c5304772a7444a3: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.24">Pro 21:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.24">24</reference> A proud and arrogant man is called mocker (free-spirit);      One who acteth in superfluity of haughtiness. <div eID="gen11479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11480" type="x-p"/> We have thus translated (vol. i. p. 39): the proverb defines almost in a formal way an idea current from the time of Solomon: לץ (properly, the distorter, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>) is an old word; but as with us in the west since the last century, the names of <hi type="italic">free-thinkers</hi> and <hi type="italic">esprits forts</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.46.12">Isa 46:12</reference>) have become current for such as subject the faith of the Church to destructive criticism, so then they were called לצים, who mockingly, as men of full age, set themselves above revealed religion and prophecy (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference>); and the above proverb gives the meaning of this name, for it describes in his moral character such a man. Thus we call one זד, haughty, and זד יהיר dna ,, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, destroying himself, and thus thoughtlessly haughty, who בּעברת זדון acts in superfluity or arrogance (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.23">Pro 11:23</reference>) of haughtiness; for not only does he inwardly raise himself above all that is worthy of recognition as true, of faith as certain, of respect as holy; but acting as well as judging frivolously, he shows reverence for nothing, scornfully passing sentence against everything. Abulwalîd (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Gesen. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.) takes יהיר in the sense of obstinate; for he compares the Arab. jahr (jahar), which is equivalent to lijâj, constancy, stubbornness. But in the Targ. and Talm. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>, Levy's <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterb</hi>. under יהיר) יהר in all its offshoots and derivations has the sense of pride; we have then rather to compare the Arab. istaihara, to be insane (= dhahb 'aḳlh, <hi type="italic">mens ejus alienata est</hi>), perhaps also to hajjir, mutahawwir, being overthrown, <hi type="italic">praeceps</hi>, so that יהיר denotes one who by his ὑπερφρονεῖν is carried beyond all σωφρονεῖν (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Rom.12.3">Rom 12:3</reference>), one who is altogether mad from pride. The Syr. madocho (Targ. מריחא), by which יהיר (Targ. יהיר) is rendered here and at <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>, is its synonym; this word also combines in itself the ideas foolhardy, and of one acting in a presumptuous, mad way; in a word, of one who is arrogant. Schultens is in the right way; but when he translates by <hi type="italic">tumidus mole cava ruens</hi>, he puts, as it is his custom to do, too much into the word; <hi type="italic">tumidus</hi>, puffed up, presents an idea which, etymologically at least, does not lie in it. The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.: ἀκρατὴς θρασὺς βωμολόχος τοὔνομά οἱ, which may be translated: an untractable reckless person we call a fool [<hi type="italic">homo ineptus</hi>], is not bad.
entries.8ceae44393cccf0c94bd984e679a29954416e9f7: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.25">Pro 21:25</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.25">25</reference> The desire of the slothful killeth him;      For his hands refuse to be active. <div eID="gen11480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11481" type="x-p"/> The desire of the עצל, Hitzig remarks, goes out first after meat and drink; and when it takes this direction, as hunger, it kills him indeed. But in this case it is not the desire that kills him, but the impossibility of satisfying it. The meaning is simply: the inordinate desire after rest and pleasure kills the slothful; for this always seeking only enjoyment and idleness brings him at last to ruin. תּאוה means here, as in <hi type="italic">Kibroth ha-tava</hi>, Num 11:34, inordinate longing after enjoyments. The proverb is connected by almost all interpreters (also Ewald, Bertheau, Hitzig, Elster, Zöckler) as a tetrastich with <reference osisRef="Prov.21.25">Pro 21:25</reference> : he (the slothful) always eagerly desires, but the righteous giveth and spareth not. But (1) although צדּיק, since it designates one who is faithful to duty, might be used particularly of the industrious (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.15.19">Pro 15:19</reference>), yet would there be wanting in 26a ואין, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.4">Pro 13:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.20.4">Pro 20:4</reference>, necessary for the formation of the contrast; (2) this older Book of Proverbs consists of pure distichs; the only tristich, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.7">Pro 19:7</reference>, appears as the consequence of a mutilation from the lxx. Thus the pretended tetrastich before us is only apparently such.
entries.dc89e7faadee8549ce670a7580f5573e2c266c34: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.26">Pro 21:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.26">26</reference> One always desireth eagerly;      But the righteous giveth and holdeth not back. <div eID="gen11481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11482" type="x-p"/> Otherwise Fleischer: <hi type="italic">per totum diem avet avidus</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">avarus</hi>; but that in התאוּה תּאוה the verb is connected with its inner obj. is manifest from Num 11:4; it is the mode of expression which is called in the Greek syntax <hi type="italic">schema etymologicum</hi>, and which is also possible without an adj. joined to the obj., as in the ὕβριν θ ̓ ὑβρίζεις (Eurip. <hi type="italic">Herc. fur</hi>. 706), the Arab. mârâhu miryatn: he had a strife with him. Euchel impossibly: necessities will continually be appeased, which would have required תּתאוּה or מתאוּה. The explanation also cannot be: each day presents its special demand, for כּל־היּום does not mean each day, but the whole day, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, continually. Thus we render התאוה with the most general subject (in which case the national grammarians supply המּתאוּה): continually one longs longing, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, there are demands, solicitations, wishes, importunate petitions; but still the righteous is not embarrassed in his generosity, he gives as unceasingly (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">Isa 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">Isa 58:1</reference>) as one asks. Thus the perf. is explained, which is related hypothetically to the fut. following: though one, etc.
entries.e510605a486ad0811d448f9a022b6934fe68fa89: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.27">Pro 21:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.27">27</reference> The sacrifice of the godless is an abomination;      How much more if it is brought for evil! <div eID="gen11482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11483" type="x-p"/> Line first = Pro 15:8. Regarding the syllogistic אף כּי, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., 12:31; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.11">Pro 15:11</reference>; regarding זמּה, crime, particularly the sin of lewdness (from זמם, to press together, to collect the thoughts upon something, to contrive, cf. <hi type="italic">raffinement de la volupté</hi>), at Pro 10:23. בּזמּה is too vaguely rendered in the lxx by παρονόμως, falsely by Jerome, <hi type="italic">ex scelere</hi> (cf. ἐξ ἀδίκου, Sir. 31:18, with Mal 1:13). The ב is not meant, as at <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.11">Eze 22:11</reference>, of the way and manner; for that the condition of life of the רשׁע is not a pure one, is not to be supposed. It is as Hitzig, rightly, that of price: for a transgression, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to atone for it; one is hereby reminded, that he who had intercourse with a betrothed bondmaid had to present an ascham [trespass-offering], <reference osisRef="Lev.19.20">Lev 19:20</reference>-22. But frequently enough would it occur that rich sensualists brought trespass-offerings, and other offerings, in order thereby to recompense for their transgressions, and to purchase for themselves the connivance of God for their dissolute life. Such offerings of the godless, the proverb means, are to God a twofold and a threefold abomination; for in this case not only does the godless fail in respect of repentance and a desire after salvation, which are the conditions of all sacrifices acceptable to God, but he makes God directly a minister of sin.
entries.f6f6cd2d139e7bb6cef3d6ff69cdf1e186e77e40: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.28">Pro 21:28</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.28">28</reference> A false witness shall perish;      But he who heareth shall always speak truth. <div eID="gen11483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11484" type="x-p"/> The lxx translate 28b by ἀνὴρ δὲ φυλασσόμενος λαλήσει. Cappellus supposes that they read לנצר for לנצה, which, however, cannot mean “taking care.” Hitzig further imagines שׂמח for שׁמע, and brings out the meaning: “the man that rejoiceth to deliver shall speak.” But where in all the world does נצר mean “to deliver”? It means, “to guard, preserve;” and to reach the meaning of “to deliver,” a clause must be added with מן, as מרע. When one who speaks lies (עד כּזבים), and a man who hears (אישׁ שּׁומע, <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, and with the orthophonic Dagesh), are contrasted, the former is one who fancifully or malevolently falsifies the fact, and the latter is one who before he speaks hears in order that he may say nothing that he has not surely heard. As לב שׁמע, 1Ki 3:9, means an obedient heart, so here אישׁ שּׁומע means a man who attentively hears, carefully proves. Such an one will speak לנצח, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, not: according to the truth, and not: for victory (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, εἰς νῖκος), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, so that accomplishes it (Oetinger); for the Heb. נצח has neither that Arab. nor this Aram. signification; but, with the transference of the root meaning of radiating or streaming over, to time, continuous existence (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Orelli, <hi type="italic">Synonyma der Zeit und Ewigkeit</hi>, pp. 96-97), thus: he will speak for continuance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, either: without ever requiring to be silent, or, which we prefer: so that what he says stands; on the contrary, he who testifies mere fictions, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, avers that they are truth, is destroyed (28a = <reference osisRef="Prov.19.9">Pro 19:9</reference>, cf. 5): he himself comes to nothing, since his testimonies are referred to their groundlessness and falsity; for שׁקר אין לו רגלים, the lie has no feet on which it can stand, it comes to nothing sooner or later.
entries.9a45f45a4fa824c8a7a18846dbd9904bfc9b4af7: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.29">Pro 21:29</reference> <div eID="gen11484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11485" type="x-p"/> Another proverb with אישׁ: - <div eID="gen11485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11486" type="x-p"/> A godless man showeth boldness in his mien; <div eID="gen11486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11487" type="x-p"/> But one that is upright-he proveth his way. <div eID="gen11487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11488" type="x-p"/> The Chethı̂b has יכין; but that the upright directeth, <hi type="italic">dirigit</hi>, his way, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, gives to it the right direction (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.6">2Ch 27:6</reference>), is not a good contrast to the boldness of the godless; the Kerı̂, הבין דּרכּו, deserves the preference. Aquila, Symmachus, the Syr., Targ., and <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. adhere to the Chethı̂b, which would be suitable if it could be translated, with Jerome, by <hi type="italic">corrigit</hi>; Luther also reads the verb with כ, but as if it were יכּון (whoever is pious, his way will stand) - only the lxx render the Kerı̂ (συνιεῖ); as for the rest, the ancients waver between the Chethı̂b דּרכיו and the Kerı̂ דּרכּו: the former refers to manner of life in general; the latter (as at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.31">Pro 3:31</reference> and elsewhere) to the conduct in separate cases; thus the one is just as appropriate as the other. In the circumstantial designation אישׁ רשׁע (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Pro 11:7</reference>) we have the stamp of the distinction of different classes of men peculiar to the Book of Proverbs. העז (to make firm, defiant) had, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">Pro 7:13</reference>, פנים as accus.; the בּ here is not that used in metaphoristic expressions instead of the accus. obj., which we have spoken of at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.4">Pro 15:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.30">Pro 20:30</reference>, but that of the means; for the face is thought of, not as the object of the action, but, after Gesen. §138, 1, as the means of its accomplishment: the godless makes (shows) firmness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, defiance, accessibility to no admonition, which is countenance; but the upright considers, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, proves (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.8">Pro 14:8</reference>), his way. בּין (הבין) means a perceiving of the object in its specific peculiarity, an understanding of its constituent parts and essential marks; it denotes knowing an event analytically, as השׂכּיל, as well as synthetically (cf. Arab. shakl), and is thus used as the expression of a perception, which apprehends the object not merely immediately, but closely examines into its circumstances. <div eID="gen11488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11489" type="x-p"/> If we further seek for the boundaries, the proverbs regarding the rich and the poor, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.2">Pro 22:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.7">Pro 22:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.16">Pro 22:16</reference>, present themselves as such, and this the more surely as <reference osisRef="Prov.22.16">Pro 22:16</reference> is without contradiction the terminus. Thus we take first together 21:30-22:2.
entries.8424aeb2027fadad65cd2428a5d993a31ef612b6: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.30">Pro 21:30</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.30">30</reference> No wisdom and no understanding,      And no counsel is there against Jahve. <div eID="gen11489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11490" type="x-p"/> The expression might also be 'לפני ה; but the predominating sense would then be, that no wisdom appears to God as such, that He values none as such. With לנגד the proverb is more objective: there is no wisdom which, compared with His, can be regarded as such (cf. <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1Co 3:19</reference>), none which can boast itself against Him, or can at all avail against Him (לנגד, as <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Dan 10:12</reference>; Neh. 3:37); whence it follows (as <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>) that the wisdom of man consists in the fear of God the Alone-wise, or, which is the same thing, the All-wise. Immanuel interprets חכמה of theology, תּבוּנה of worldly science, עצה of politics; but חכמה is used of the knowledge of truth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of that which truly is and continues; תבונה of criticism, and עצה of system and method; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.2">Pro 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.14">Pro 8:14</reference>, from which latter passage the lxx has substituted here גבורה instead of תבונה. Instead of 'לנגד ה it translates πρὸς τὸν ἀσεβῆ, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, for that which is 'נגד ה against Jahve.
entries.7797391aeeb0cc60b59442ceb25e135e18516e2a: <reference osisRef="Prov.21.31">Pro 21:31</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.31">31</reference> The horse is harnessed for the day of battle;      But with Jahve is the victory, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it remains with Him to give the victory or not, for the horse is a vain means of victory, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.17">Isa 33:17</reference>; the battle is the Lord's, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">1Sa 17:47</reference>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it depends on Him how the battle shall issue; and king and people who have taken up arms in defence of their rights have thus to trust nothing in the multitude of their war-horses (סוּס, horses, including their riders), and generally in their preparations for the battle, but in the Lord (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference>, and, on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">Isa 31:1</reference>). The lxx translates התּשׁוּעה by ἡ βοήθεια, as if the Arab. name of victory, naṣr, proceeding from this fundamental meaning, stood in the text; תשׁועה (from ישׁע, Arab. ws', to be wide, to have free space for motion) signifies properly prosperity, as the contrast of distress, oppression, slavery, and victory (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.10">Psa 144:10</reference>, and ישׁוּעה, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sa 14:45</reference>). The post-bibl. Heb. uses נצח (נצּחון) for victory; but the O.T. Heb. has no word more fully covering this idea than תשׁועה (ישׁועה).<note placement="foot">Note: In the old High German, the word for war is <hi type="italic">urlag</hi> (<hi type="italic">urlac</hi>), fate, because the issue is the divine determination, and <hi type="italic">nôt</hi> (as in “<hi type="italic">der Nibelunge Not</hi>”), as binding, confining, restraint; this <hi type="italic">nôt</hi> is the correlate to תשׁועה, victory; מלחמה corresponds most to the French <hi type="italic">guerre</hi>, which is not of Romanic, but of German origin: the <hi type="italic">Werre</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Gewirre</hi> [complication, confusion], for נלחם signifies to press against one another, to be engaged in close conflict; cf. the Homeric κλόνος of the turmoil of battle.</note>  <chapter eID="Prov.21"/> <div eID="gen11490" type="x-p"/>
