                  <ns0:p n="1">1 THe kings heart <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">His very inward purposes and inclinations, which seem to be most in a Man's own power, and out of the reach of all others, and much more his Tongue and Hand, and all his outward actions. He names <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> hot to exclude other men, but because they are more arbitrary and uncontrollable than other men.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the hand of the LORD, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the rivers of water <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which Husbandmen or Gardiners can draw by little Channels into the adjacent grounds as they please, and as their occasions require.</ns0:note>, he turneth it <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Directeth and boweth partly by suggesting those things to their Minds which have a commanding influence upon their wills, and partly by a direct and immediate motion of their wills and affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons, which being God's Creatures must needs be as subject to his power and pleasure as either mens Minds or Bodies are, and which he moves sweetly and suitably to their own Nature, though strongly and effectually.</ns0:note> whi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thersoever he will <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So as they shall fulfil his counsels and designs, either of Mercy or of Correction to themselves, or to their People.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Every way of a man <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> right in his own eyes, but the LORD pondereth the hearts <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This was said, Ch. 16. 2. where it is explained, and is here repeated, either for the great importance and usefulness of it, or because he perceived that the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were very prone to self<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deceit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Mic. 6. 7, 8.</ns0:note> To do justice and judgment <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The conscientious performance of all our duties to men.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> more accepta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to the LORD than sacrifice <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Than the most costly, outward services offered to God, joyned with the neglect of our Moral duties to God or men. The same thing is affirmed, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 15. 22. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 6. 6. <ns0:hi>Mic.</ns0:hi> 6. 7, 8, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> haugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiness of eyes.</ns0:note> An high look <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">One gesture or sign of Pride put for all the rest. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 6. 17.</ns0:note>, and a proud heart <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Pride lurking and reigning in the Heart, though it do not discover it self to men by outward actions, but be disguised with a shew<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of humility, as it is frequently.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> the light of the wicked.</ns0:note> the plowing <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either 1. strictly and properly so called: even their civil or natural actions, which in themselves are lawful and good, are made sinful as they are ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naged by ungodly men, without any regard to the service and glory of God, which ought to be the great end of all our actions, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10. 31. and with a design of serving their own wicked lusts by it. Or 2. Metaphorically, their designs and endeavours, which are said to be <ns0:hi>sin,</ns0:hi> because they are wholly and fully set upon sin, and they make sin their trade or business, which is called <ns0:hi>Plowing wickedness,</ns0:hi> Job 4. 8. But all the ancient Interpreters, and divers others render the word <ns0:hi>the Lamp</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Light,</ns0:hi> as this Hebrew word, even thus pointed, is rendred, 1 Kings 11. 36. & 15. 4. 2 Kings 8. 19. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 21. 7. and the <ns0:hi>Lamp of the wicked</ns0:hi> is a Phrase used in this Book, Ch. 13. 9. & 24. 20. as also, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 21. 17. whereas <ns0:hi>the Plowing of the wicked</ns0:hi> is a Phrase not elsewhere used. And this seems best to agree with the Context, for by their <ns0:hi>Lamp</ns0:hi> he seems to understand all their pomp and glory, that worldly great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and Prosperity, which is the Fewel of their Pride, and therefore is most fitly joyned with it.</ns0:note> of the wicked, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> sin <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It is by them turned into sin, and made the occasion of much wickedness.                   <ns0:p n="7">7 The robbery of the wicked shall <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>saw them,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>dwell with them.</ns0:hi>
